links.outcome: Accuracy of sources and citations in LLM reasoning outputs, verified by two raters
links.effect: Citation accuracy was 76% for GPT-4 versus 19% for Mixtral-8x7B; correct predictions could rest on hallucinated knowledge and inaccurate citation.
links.quote: Additionally, Fig. 3 (d) demonstrates GPT-4’s superior citation accuracy (76% for GPT-4 vs. 19% for Mixtral), indicating GPT-4’s enhanced ability to provide evidence-based sources for its decision.

links.outcome: Performance sensitivity to input variation: narrative length, persona prompt, and language
links.effect: Performance varied with description length (U-shaped, up to 32%), persona (GPT-4 +13.68%), and language (Mixtral -8% in same-language non-English setting; GPT-4 -1.4%, n.s.).
links.quote: However, in the same-language setting (non-English symptoms and prompt), Mixtral’s performance declines substantially by 8%, while GPT-4 remains stable (-1.4%, n.s.).

links.outcome: Calibration and confidence of LLM likelihood outputs versus correctness
links.effect: Confidence and Brier calibration improved with prompt engineering (FS-CoT, SC best); GPT-4 best calibrated even zero-shot, but high confidence does not guarantee correctness.
links.quote: Notably, GPT-4 shows the best calibration, even in the zero-shot condition.

links.outcome: Correctness of LLM clinical knowledge recall and reasoning rated by epileptologist
links.effect: GPT-4 knowledge recall errors 17.28% vs Mixtral 43.21%; Mixtral incorrect reasoning 38.27% vs GPT-4 20.99%; correct output 56.79% vs 29.63%.
links.quote: When examining specific dimensions (Fig. 3 (c)), GPT-4 made fewer errors for knowledge recall than Mixtral (17.28% vs. 43.21%; z-test for proportions, p <0.05).

links.outcome: LLM F1 for seizure onset zone localization compared with clinicians and naive baseline
links.effect: Zero-shot F1 of GPT-4 52.27% and Mixtral 51.66% versus clinicians 48.77% and 46.75%; naive classifier 38.21%.
links.quote: Exceptions are Mixtral-8 × 7B and GPT-4, which achieved substantially higher F1 scores than all other models of 51.66% and 52.27%, respectively (95% CI: [51.43, 51.90], [52.04, 52.50]), comparable to the clinician’s performance: Clinician 1 - 48.77% (95% CI: [48.53, 49.02]) and Clinician 2 - 46.75% (95% CI: [46.51, 46.99]).

links.outcome: SOZ localization accuracy against ground truth
links.effect: Top zero-shot F1 was 51.66% for Mixtral and 52.27% for GPT-4, versus clinicians 48.77% and 46.75%.
links.quote: Exceptions are Mixtral-8 × 7B and GPT-4, which achieved substantially higher F1 scores than all other models of 51.66% and 52.27%, respectively (95% CI: [51.43, 51.90], [52.04, 52.50]), comparable to the clinician’s performance: Clinician 1 - 48.77% (95% CI: [48.53, 49.02]) and Clinician 2 - 46.75% (95% CI: [46.51, 46.99]).

links.outcome: model F1 versus clinicians
links.effect: GPT-4 and Mixtral achieved 52.27% and 51.66% F1, comparable to clinicians at 48.77% and 46.75%.
links.quote: Exceptions are Mixtral-8 × 7B and GPT-4, which achieved substantially higher F1 scores than all other models of 51.66% and 52.27%, respectively (95% CI: [51.43, 51.90], [52.04, 52.50]), comparable to the clinician’s performance: Clinician 1 - 48.77% (95% CI: [48.53, 49.02]) and Clinician 2 - 46.75% (95% CI: [46.51, 46.99]).

links.outcome: expert-rated reasoning correctness and completeness
links.effect: In 81 CoT responses, GPT-4 correctness/completeness 56.79%/65.00% vs Mixtral 29.63%/34.57%, p<0.05.
links.quote: As shown in Fig. 3 (b) GPT-4 significantly outperformed Mixtral in both correctness (56.79% vs. 29.63%; z-test for proportions, p <0.05) and completeness (65.00% vs. 34.57%; z-test for proportions, p <0.05).

links.outcome: hallucinated reasoning and inaccurate citations
links.effect: Clinical experts found correct predictions could rely on hallucinated knowledge and inaccurate source citation.
links.quote: However, reasoning analysis by clinical experts reveal that correct prediction can be based on hallucinated knowledge and inaccurate source citation, underscoring the need to improve interpretability of LLMs in clinical use.

links.outcome: source citation accuracy
links.effect: Citation accuracy was 76% for GPT-4 and 19% for Mixtral.
links.quote: Additionally, Fig. 3 (d) demonstrates GPT-4’s superior citation accuracy (76% for GPT-4 vs. 19% for Mixtral), indicating GPT-4’s enhanced ability to provide evidence-based sources for its decision.

links.outcome: calibration of likelihood estimates
links.effect: Zero-shot calibration showed high variance; refined prompting markedly improved calibration for all models.
links.quote: As shown in Fig. 2 (b) top, models exhibit a high variance in calibration in the zero-shot condition.

links.outcome: performance under input and language variations
links.effect: Performance variation was 13.7% for persona, 32.7% for narrative length, and 14.2% for language context.
links.quote: Performance is further strongly modulated by clinical in-context impersonation, narrative length and language context (13.7%, 32.7% and 14.2% performance variation, respectively).

links.outcome: F1 across prompt strategies
links.effect: Median F1 improvement vs zero-shot: Few-Shot 6.49%, CoT 9.62%, FS-CoT 9.49%, SC 10.02%.
links.quote: Importantly, we observed a substantial performance increase when introducing prompt-engineering across all models: Median F1 improvement relative to ZS was 6.49% for Few-Shot prompting, 9.62% for CoT, 9.49% in FS-CoT, and 10.02% increase for SC.
